docs.title: Extension
docs.text:
MQTT is a lightweight publish/subscribe messaging protocol designed for M2M (machine to machine) telemetry in low bandwidth environments. Fastapi-mqtt is the client for working with MQTT.

For more information about MQTT, please refer to here: MQTT

Fastapi-mqtt wraps around the gmqtt module, a Python async MQTT client. The module supports the MQTT version 5.0 protocol.

docs.title: Available Features
docs.text:
• Subscribe to topics with decorated handlers, publish to topics
  • Pydantic models for message payloads, to receive and publish typed messages
  • MQTT 5.0, with callbacks for connection events
  • MQTT settings with a pydantic class, authentication to the broker with credentials

docs.title: Connection callbacks
docs.text:
Besides @mqtt.subscribe(...), these decorators give access to the low-level MQTT events:

from typing import Any

from gmqtt import Client as MQTTClient


@mqtt.on_connect()
def connect(client: MQTTClient, flags: int, rc: int, properties: Any):
    print("Connected: ", client, flags, rc, properties)


@mqtt.on_message()
async def message(client: MQTTClient, topic: str, payload: bytes, qos: int, properties: Any):
    print("Received message: ", topic, payload.decode(), qos, properties)


@mqtt.on_disconnect()
def disconnect(client: MQTTClient, packet, exc=None):
    print("Disconnected")


@mqtt.on_subscribe()
def subscribe(client: MQTTClient, mid: int, qos: int, properties: Any):
    print("subscribed", client, mid, qos, properties)
  • on_connect runs after every successful (re)connection to the broker.
  • on_message gets every message the client receives, from all its subscriptions. The @mqtt.subscribe(...) handlers of the topic run too.
  • on_disconnect runs when the connection is lost or closed.
  • on_subscribe runs when the broker confirms a subscription.

Topics can also be subscribed directly with the gmqtt client, for example in on_connect with client.subscribe("topic"). Their messages only reach on_message.

docs.title: Registering handlers after startup
docs.text: Handlers are usually registered at module level, before mqtt_startup(). Handlers registered later also work: topics are subscribed right away, and on_connect handlers are called right away with the current connection.

docs.title: Unsubscribe
docs.text:
mqtt.unsubscribe("sensors/+/temperature")

The topic is unsubscribed from the broker, and its handlers are removed.

docs.title: Shutdown reason code
docs.text:
mqtt_shutdown() accepts an optional MQTT 5.0 DISCONNECT reason code and properties:

await mqtt.mqtt_shutdown(reason_code=4, reason_string="shutting down")

docs.title: Will message
docs.text:
The will message is a message the broker publishes for the client if it disconnects abnormally, like when the app crashes or loses its network. It's set up in the config, and sent to the broker when connecting:

mqtt_config = MQTTConfig(
    will_message_topic="status/my-app",
    will_message_payload="offline",
    will_delay_interval=2,
)

On a normal shutdown the will message is not published. To publish it anyway, shut down with reason code 4 (disconnect with will message):

await mqtt.mqtt_shutdown(reason_code=4)

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
from fastapi_mqtt import FastMQTT, MQTTConfig

mqtt_config = MQTTConfig(
    host="mqtt.example.com",
    port=1883,
    keepalive=60,
    username="username",
    password="strong_password",
)
mqtt = FastMQTT(config=mqtt_config)

docs.title: MQTTConfig class
docs.text:
The class has the following attributes:

  • host: To connect MQTT broker, defaults to localhost

  • port: To connect MQTT broker, defaults to 1883

  • ssl: an SSL/TLS transport is created (by default a plain TCP transport is created) In case of an ssl.SSLContext object, context is used to create the transport. Alternately passing bool value, will set a default context, which is calls ssl.create_default_context().

  • keepalive: Maximum period in seconds between communications with the broker. This controls the rate at which the client will send ping messages. Defaults to 60 seconds.

  • username: username for authentication, defaults to None

  • password: password for authentication, defaults to None

  • version: MQTT broker version to use, defaults to MQTTv50. According to gmqtt.Client if the broker does not support 5.0 protocol version, responds with proper CONNACK reason code, the client will downgrade to 3.1 and reconnect automatically.

  • reconnect_retries: Number of failed reconnect attempts allowed after a lost connection, before giving up (gmqtt makes one more attempt than this number). Defaults to -1, which means unlimited attempts.

  • reconnect_delay: Delay in seconds between reconnect attempts, defaults to 6. For more info: gmqtt reconnects

The last three parameters are used after the client disconnects abnormally, see will message:

  • will_message_topic: Topic of the payload
  • will_message_payload: The payload
  • will_delay_interval: Delay interval

docs.title: FastMQTT params
docs.text:
The client has the following parameters:

  • config: MQTTConfig config object

  • client_id: Should be a unique identifier for connection to the MQTT broker.

  • clean_session: Enables broker to establish a persistent session. In a persistent session clean_session = False. The broker stores all subscriptions for the client. If the session is not persistent (clean_session = True). The broker does not store anything for the client and purges all information from any previous persistent session. The client_id identifies the session.

  • optimistic_acknowledgement: If True (default), QoS 1/2 messages are acknowledged before the message handlers run. If False, they are acknowledged after the handlers finish. Only applies to MQTT 5.0.

  • mqtt_logger: Optional logging.Logger to use.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text:
Please refer to each project's style and contribution guidelines for submitting patches and additions. In general, we follow the "fork-and-pull" Git workflow.

  1. Fork the repo on GitHub
  2. Clone the project to your own machine
  3. Commit changes to your own branch
  4. Push your work
  5. Submit a Pull request so that we can review your changes

docs.title: Before contributing, here is how to install
docs.text:
Requirements: Python 3.12+ and Poetry 2.x.

git clone https://github.com/sabuhish/fastapi-mqtt.git
cd fastapi-mqtt
poetry install
# activate the poetry virtualenv
eval $(poetry env activate)
# to make changes and validate them
pre-commit install
pre-commit run --all-files

docs.title: Running tests
docs.text:
Tests need an MQTT broker. Run a local one with Docker, the same version used in CI:

docker run -d --rm --name mqtt -p 1883:1883 eclipse-mosquitto:1.6.15
pytest
docker stop mqtt

To run the tests against another broker, set its host in TEST_BROKER_HOST, like TEST_BROKER_HOST=test.mosquitto.org pytest for the public test broker.

Explore the fastapi app examples and run them with uvicorn

uvicorn examples.app:app --port 8000 --reload

NOTE: Be sure to merge the latest from "upstream" before making a pull request!

docs.title: Code formatting
docs.text:
This project uses pre-commit to apply multiple linters to the code changes before they're committed.

You can invoke it anytime by running pre-commit run --all-files.

Install the git hook with pre-commit install to trigger it when committing changes.

docs.title: Full example
docs.text:
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager

from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi_mqtt.config import MQTTConfig
from fastapi_mqtt.fastmqtt import FastMQTT

fast_mqtt = FastMQTT(config=MQTTConfig())


@asynccontextmanager
async def _lifespan(_app: FastAPI):
    await fast_mqtt.mqtt_startup()
    yield
    await fast_mqtt.mqtt_shutdown()


app = FastAPI(lifespan=_lifespan)


@fast_mqtt.on_connect()
def connect(client, flags, rc, properties):
    fast_mqtt.client.subscribe("mqtt")  # subscribing mqtt topic
    print("Connected: ", client, flags, rc, properties)


@fast_mqtt.on_message()
async def message(client, topic, payload, qos, properties):
    print("Received message: ", topic, payload.decode(), qos, properties)
    return 0


@fast_mqtt.subscribe("my/mqtt/topic/#")
async def message_to_topic(client, topic, payload, qos, properties):
    print("Received message to specific topic: ", topic, payload.decode(), qos, properties)


@fast_mqtt.on_disconnect()
def disconnect(client, packet, exc=None):
    print("Disconnected")


@fast_mqtt.on_subscribe()
def subscribe(client, mid, qos, properties):
    print("subscribed", client, mid, qos, properties)


@app.get("/")
async def func():
    fast_mqtt.publish("mqtt", "Hello from Fastapi")  # publishing mqtt topic

    return {"result": True, "message": "Published"}

docs.title: Example with pydantic models
docs.text:
The same Temperature model is used for the API body, for publishing and for receiving. Invalid messages go to the on_payload_error handler.

from contextlib import asynccontextmanager

from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError

from fastapi_mqtt import FastMQTT, MQTTConfig

mqtt_config = MQTTConfig()

fast_mqtt = FastMQTT(config=mqtt_config)


@asynccontextmanager
async def _lifespan(_app: FastAPI):
    await fast_mqtt.mqtt_startup()
    yield
    await fast_mqtt.mqtt_shutdown()


app = FastAPI(lifespan=_lifespan)


class Temperature(BaseModel):
    sensor: str
    value: float


# last temperature received from each sensor
latest: dict[str, Temperature] = {}


@fast_mqtt.subscribe("sensors/+/temperature", qos=1)
async def temperature(item: Temperature, topic: str):
    """The payload arrives parsed and validated as a Temperature."""
    print("Received temperature: ", topic, item)
    latest[item.sensor] = item


@fast_mqtt.on_payload_error()
async def invalid_payload(client, topic: str, payload: bytes, error: ValidationError):
    """Messages that are not a valid Temperature come here, instead of to the handler."""
    print("Invalid message on", topic, error.errors(include_input=False))


@app.post("/temperature")
async def send_temperature(item: Temperature):
    """The same model is used for the API body and for the MQTT message."""
    fast_mqtt.publish(f"sensors/{item.sensor}/temperature", item, qos=1)
    return {"result": True, "message": "Published"}


@app.get("/temperature")
async def get_temperatures() -> dict[str, Temperature]:
    return latest

Run it against a local broker, and publish a temperature through the API:

uvicorn examples.app_models:app --port 8000
curl -X POST localhost:8000/temperature -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"sensor": "kitchen", "value": 21.5}'
curl localhost:8000/temperature

docs.title: More complex examples
docs.text: Visit the examples folder for more code examples, including a full fastAPI app organized in multiple files (splitting dependencies, routes, app creation) implementing a dynamic MQTT client through a WebSocket connection.

docs.title: 🕹 Getting Started
docs.text:
After installing the module you set up your FastApi app.

The main classes are FastMQTT and MQTTConfig. The client connects to the broker in the app lifespan:

from contextlib import asynccontextmanager

from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi_mqtt import FastMQTT, MQTTConfig

mqtt_config = MQTTConfig(host="localhost", port=1883)

mqtt = FastMQTT(config=mqtt_config)


@asynccontextmanager
async def _lifespan(_app: FastAPI):
    await mqtt.mqtt_startup()
    yield
    await mqtt.mqtt_shutdown()


app = FastAPI(lifespan=_lifespan)

See Configuration for all the connection options.

docs.title: Subscribe
docs.text:
Decorate a handler with @mqtt.subscribe(...) to receive the messages of one or more topics. Topics can use the MQTT wildcards + (one level) and # (all levels below):

@mqtt.subscribe("sensors/+/temperature", "sensors/+/humidity", qos=1)
async def sensor_message(client, topic, payload, qos, properties):
    print("Received: ", topic, payload.decode(), qos, properties)

The handler gets the client, the topic of the message, the payload as bytes, the QoS level and the MQTT 5.0 properties.

Subscriptions made with the decorator are renewed automatically when the client reconnects. Payloads can also be received as pydantic models, see Pydantic Models.

docs.title: Publish
docs.text:
Publish a message to a topic, for example from a FastAPI endpoint:

@app.post("/hello")
async def hello():
    mqtt.publish("greetings", "Hello from FastAPI")
    return {"result": True, "message": "Published"}

publish also takes qos and retain arguments, and accepts pydantic models as payload.

docs.text: Python 3.12 or newer.

docs.title: Using pip or poetry
docs.text:
python3 -m venv .venv

source .venv/bin/activate

pip install fastapi-mqtt

Alternatively, if you prefer to use poetry for package dependencies:

poetry add fastapi-mqtt

docs.title: Pydantic Models
docs.text: Message payloads can be typed with pydantic models, both to receive and to publish them.

docs.title: Receiving
docs.text:
A subscription handler gets the payload parsed into a pydantic model, by typing one of its parameters with the model. The parameter name doesn't matter.

from pydantic import BaseModel


class Temperature(BaseModel):
    sensor: str
    value: float


@mqtt.subscribe("sensors/+/temperature")
async def temperature(item: Temperature):
    print(item.sensor, item.value)

The other parameters are then passed by name, so the handler can ask for any of client, topic, payload (the raw bytes), qos and properties:

@mqtt.subscribe("sensors/+/temperature")
async def temperature(item: Temperature, topic: str):
    print(topic, item.value)
  • Handlers without a model parameter get (client, topic, payload, qos, properties), as before.
  • One model per message: type the parameter with the model itself. Item | None, Optional[Item] or list[Item] are not supported. For a JSON list, use a RootModel: class Items(RootModel[list[Item]]), and read the list from items.root.
  • A handler with more than one model parameter, a model inside other types, or a parameter that is not one of the names above, raises a TypeError when it is registered.

docs.title: Invalid payloads
docs.text:
Messages with a payload that is not valid JSON for the model are skipped by that handler. Other handlers of the same topic still get them. By default they are logged as a warning, with the invalid fields but without their values, which may hold sensitive data.

To handle them yourself, register a payload error handler. It gets the pydantic ValidationError, and replaces the warning:

from pydantic import ValidationError


@mqtt.on_payload_error()
async def invalid_payload(client, topic: str, payload: bytes, error: ValidationError):
    print("Invalid message on", topic, error.errors())

The handler can be async or not.

docs.title: Publishing
docs.text:
publish accepts a pydantic model, and sends it as JSON:

mqtt.publish("sensors/kitchen/temperature", Temperature(sensor="kitchen", value=21.5))

To customize the JSON, like with exclude_none=True, call model_dump_json(...) yourself and publish the resulting string.

docs.title: With FastAPI
docs.text:
The same model can be used for the API and for MQTT:

@app.post("/temperature")
async def send_temperature(item: Temperature):
    mqtt.publish(f"sensors/{item.sensor}/temperature", item)
    return {"result": True}

docs.title: Short information about Message Queuing Telemetry Transport
docs.text:
We will cover some basics and later on will dive in advance. This information is for beginners and for those who want to gain more knowledge. If you don't have any knowledge of what MQTT does, go ahead you will get much more.

MQTT stands for Message Queuing Telemetry Transport. The protocol was invented by IBM to facilitate machine-to-machine communication. It works on the publish and subscribe model to ensure efficient communication across platforms, and also has a level system for message priority. Currently, this protocol is widely used for IoT and large-scale communication because of its small footprint and minimal bandwidth consumption.

In addition, it is designed as a lightweight messaging protocol that uses publish/subscribe operations to exchange data between clients and the server. Furthermore, its small size, low power usage, minimized data packets, and ease of implementation make the protocol ideal for the machine-to-machine or Internet of Things world.

The compact header size of MQTT and its QoS (Quality of Service) are geared toward reliable M2M communication at a fundamental level, requiring few workarounds to operate smoothly. QoS in MQTT means that each message has three levels of a check for guaranteed message delivery. The levels increase bandwidth usage as they progress, but higher QoS carries with it assurances at the highest level for critical transmissions.

So to sum up above:

  • It's a lightweight protocol. So, it's easy to implement in software and fast in data transmission.
  • It's based on a messaging technique.
  • Minimized data packets. Hence, low network usage.
  • Low power usage. As a result, it saves the connected device's battery.
  • It's real-time! That is specifically what makes it perfect for IoT applications.

docs.title: MQTT Components
docs.text:
• Broker, which is the server that handles the data transmission between the clients.
  • A topic, is the place a device wants to put or retrieve a message to/from.
  • The message (payload), is the data that a device receives when subscribing to a topic or sends when publishing to a topic.
  • Publish, is the process a device does to send its message to the broker.
  • Subscribe, where a device does to retrieve a message from the broker.

In MQTT a publisher publishes messages on a topic and a subscriber must subscribe to that topic to view the message. MQTT is based on clients and a server. Likewise, the server is the guy who is responsible for handling the client's requests for receiving or sending data between each other. MQTT server is called a broker and the clients are simply the connected devices. When a device (a client) wants to send data to the broker, we call this operation a publish. When a device (a client) wants to receive data from the broker, we call this operation a subscribe. These clients are publishing and subscribing to topics. So, the broker here is the one that handles the publishing/subscribing actions to the target topics.

docs.title: For instance
docs.text: The device has a temperature sensor. Certainly, it wants to send his readings to the broker. On the other side, a phone/desktop application wants to receive this temperature value. Therefore, 2 things will happen: The device defines the topic it wants to publish on, ex: 'temp', then, it publishes the message 'temperature value'. The phone/desktop application subscribes to the topic 'temp', it receives the message that the device has published, which is the temperature value. Again, the broker's role here is to take the message 'temperature value' and deliver it to the phone/desktop application.

docs.title: Important Points to note
docs.text:
• Clients do not have addresses like in email systems, and messages are not sent to clients.
  • Messages are published to a broker on a topic.
  • The job of an MQTT broker is to filter messages based on topic and then distribute them to subscribers.
  • A client can receive these messages by subscribing to that topic on the same broker.
  • There is no direct connection between a publisher and a subscriber.
  • All clients can publish (broadcast) and subscribe (receive).
  • MQTT brokers do not normally store messages.

docs.title: MQTT Topic
docs.text: Publishers publish to a broker, and the subscribers subscribe to that same broker and they subscribe to the same topic. They will receive all messages sent by that publisher. Publisher publishes throughout the topic and subscribers listen to the same topic to retrieve it. Topics are created dynamically when someone subscribes to a topic or someone publishes a message to a topic with the retained message set to True.

docs.title: Important Notes
docs.text:
• Topic names are case sensitive.
  • Use UTF-8.
  • Must consist of at least one character to be valid.
  • Topics do not need to begin with a / and in fact, stating your topic structure with a / is considered bad practice.

docs.title: Subscribing to Topics
docs.text:
The following are all valid topic structures for houses with sensors in several rooms. It is a design choice.

house/room1/sensor1
house/room2/sensor1
house-room1-sensor1
house-room2-sensor1
house/room1-sensor1
house/room2-sensor1

When subscribing to multiple topics two wildcard characters can be used. Wildcards can only be used to denote a level or multi-levels i.e: house/#.

# (hash character) - multi-level wildcard
+ (plus character) - single-level wildcard

docs.title: Wildcards
docs.text:
The client can subscribe to an individual or multiple topics. For multiple, you can use wild characters - # multi-level wildcard. For single-level - + single-level character. Wildcards can only be used to denote level or multi-levels: i.e: house/# subscribes you to all topics under house/.

Invalid Topic Subscriptions:

house+ - Reason no topic level
house# - Reason no topic level

Using wildcards: Subscribing to topic house/+/main-light which subscribes to any of these topics and this time ones below room1, room2 garage covered by + single. You will notice they all end with main-light.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
house/room1/main-light
house/room2/main-light
house/garage/main-light

But it does not cover:

house/room1/side-light
house/room2/side-light

Because it has a side-light, it is not main-light.

docs.title: Publishing to Topics
docs.text: A client can only publish to an individual topic. That is, using wildcards when publishing is not allowed. To publish a message to two topics you need to publish the message twice.

docs.title: MQTT Protocol
docs.text:
In comparison to HTTP, MQTT Protocol ensures high delivery guarantees. According to measurements in 3G networks, the throughput of MQTT is 93 times faster than HTTP.

There are 3 levels of Quality of Services:

  • At most once: guarantees a best-effort delivery.
  • At least once: guaranteed that a message will be delivered at least once. But the message can also be delivered more than once.
  • Exactly once: guarantees that each message is received only once by the counterpart

HTTP is a request-response protocol for client-server computing and is not always optimized for mobile devices. The main solid benefits of MQTT in these terms are light weightiness (MQTT transfers data as a byte array) and publish/subscribe model, which makes it perfect for resource-constrained devices and helps to save battery. MQTT is a binary-based protocol where the control elements are binary bytes and not text strings. MQTT has a very short message header and the smallest packet message size of 2 bytes.

docs.title: MQTT specification
docs.text:
• CONNECT
  • PUBLISH
  • SUBSCRIBE
  • UNSUBSCRIBE
  • DISCONNECT

Whereas HTTP specifications are much longer. HTTP is worthy and extendable. But MQTT is more suitable when it is referred to as IoT development.

MQTT uses a command and command acknowledgment format. That means each command has an associated acknowledgment. Topic names, Client ID, username, and passwords are encoded as UTF-8 strings. The Payload excluding MQTT protocol information like Client ID etc. is binary data and the content and format are application-specific. The fixed header field consists of the control field and the variable-length packet length field.

The MQTT packet or message format consists of a 2-byte fixed header (always present) + Variable-header (not always present)+ payload (not always present). It is interesting that the client ID field is sent as the first part of the payload, and not as part of the header. MQTT uses TCP/IP to connect to the broker. TCP is a connection-orientated protocol with error correction and guarantees that packets are received in order.
